I’m checking Claude Code’s current hook lifecycle against the controls our projection needs: intercepting provider context, injecting a task card, observing tool results, persisting audit data, and replacing/removing old messages. The last item is the decisive one.

Not through Claude Code hooks alone—not with the same level of control we have in Pi.

Claude hooks provide most of the observation layer, but not the crucial provider-context projection layer.

What Claude hooks can do:

- Read the complete session transcript through `transcript_path`.
- Detect new prompts with `UserPromptSubmit`.
- Observe tool batches through `PostToolBatch`.
- Capture individual results with `PostToolUse`.
- Replace a tool result before Claude initially sees it using `updatedToolOutput`.
- Inject a task card using `additionalContext`.
- Detect session resume, clear, and compact events.
- Persist our event log, evidence versions, leases, and audits externally.  
  [Claude Code hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)

The critical limitation is that hooks cannot rewrite the provider message list before every model request. They cannot remove:

- A file read Claude saw earlier.
- An old injected task card.
- A consumed tool result.
- Previous conversation turns.

In fact, Claude’s documentation says context returned by multiple hooks is retained and combined. Continuously injecting refreshed cards would cause old cards to accumulate—the opposite of our goal. [Claude hooks guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide)

`PreCompact` also isn’t sufficient. It can observe or block compaction, but cannot replace Claude’s generated compact summary. `PostCompact` can only observe the result. [Compaction hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#precompact)

### What we could build

A Claude-compatible “task card lite” could:

- Store the immutable evidence log and leases.
- Inject a small card on `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, resume, and after compaction.
- Replace extremely noisy tool outputs immediately through `PostToolUse`.
- Preserve full tool output externally while returning a bounded extract.
- Recommend or automate a fresh-session workflow when an unrelated task begins.
- Audit context behavior and warn about repeated reads.

This could reduce tokens, but it cannot produce Pi’s sawtooth context inside an ordinary Claude session because previously delivered messages remain present.

### Full equivalent

A true equivalent would require one of these:

1. Anthropic adds a before-model-request hook that can return a replacement message array.
2. We run Claude through our own Agent SDK wrapper and manage each provider request/context ourselves.
3. We intentionally start fresh Claude sessions at task or turn boundaries, injecting our projection into each new session.

Option 2 is the closest architectural match, but it becomes a Claude Code wrapper rather than a normal hook/plugin.

So: the extraction engine is portable, but the Pi integration mechanism is not. Hooks are enough for a useful Claude edition, perhaps 50–70% of the benefit, but not enough to honestly claim identical behavior.

Yes — and it's actually a *better* fit for the "adapt to whatever hardware is present" goal than our current ONNX/DirectML setup. Here's how it works, with sources:

**GPU layer offload is a graceful, tunable knob, not all-or-nothing.** `n_gpu_layers` (`GpuLayerCount` in LLamaSharp) controls how many of the model's transformer layers get placed on GPU vs CPU. `-1` means "try to offload everything." If the GPU doesn't have enough VRAM for all layers, llama.cpp offloads what fits and keeps the rest on CPU automatically — a partial fallback, not a crash ([n_gpu_layers guide](https://bmdpat.com/blog/llama-cpp-n-gpu-layers-explained-2026), [llama.cpp multi-GPU docs](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/multi-gpu.md)).

**The important nuance for our specific goal:** LLamaSharp ships separate backend NuGet packages — `LLamaSharp.Backend.Cpu` (CPU everywhere, plus Metal on Mac), `.Cuda11`/`.Cuda12` (NVIDIA, Windows+Linux), `.Vulkan` (broad GPU coverage — AMD/Intel/NVIDIA, Windows+Linux). Unlike our current ONNX setup where the RID-conditional `.csproj` picks exactly **one** backend at publish time and that's what ships, **you can bundle multiple LLamaSharp backend packages together in one app**, and it auto-selects the right native library for whatever machine it's actually running on at runtime ([NuGet docs](https://www.nuget.org/packages/LLamaSharp), [SciSharp/LLamaSharp#456](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/issues/456)). That's a genuinely cleaner match for "one shipped artifact, adapts to GPU/NPU/CPU automatically" than what we have now.

**One real caveat to design around:** if you only install the CPU-only backend package, GPU-related settings are silently accepted and do nothing — you don't get real GPU support unless the GPU-capable backend is actually bundled ([source](https://bmdpat.com/blog/llama-cpp-n-gpu-layers-explained-2026)). So the plan would be: ship CPU + Vulkan (broadest GPU coverage) as the default bundle, `GpuLayerCount = -1` by default, safe fallback built in.

I didn't find anything suggesting LoRA-plus-GPU-offload has a fundamental limitation (it's a mainstream, widely-used combination) — the `CPU_REPACK` fallback warnings we saw in the test were a CPU-only quantization-layout detail, unrelated to GPU.

Sources:
- [llama.cpp --n-gpu-layers Guide](https://bmdpat.com/blog/llama-cpp-n-gpu-layers-explained-2026)
- [llama.cpp multi-gpu.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/multi-gpu.md)
- [LLamaSharp on NuGet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/LLamaSharp)
- [SciSharp/LLamaSharp#456 — backend selection](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/issues/456)

Antigravity is the closest native target because it has a true `PreInvocation` event before every model call; Cursor has recently expanded cloud-agent conversation hooks; Codex supports customization hooks but does not expose the message-array projection point. Here’s the practical ranking for porting the task-card architecture:

| Platform | Before every model call | Inject fresh card | Remove old context | Verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Pi | Yes | Yes | Yes | Full implementation |

### Antigravity

This is the most promising next target.

Its `PreInvocation` hook fires before every model call, provides the transcript path and invocation number, and can inject an `ephemeralMessage`. That is almost perfectly shaped for supplying a freshly extracted task card without permanently storing each card in the trajectory. [Antigravity hooks](https://antigravity.google/docs/hooks)

The missing control is deletion: `PreInvocation` can return `injectSteps`, but the documented schema cannot replace or remove existing trajectory steps. Therefore:

- Fresh card injection: yes.
- Immutable transcript analysis: yes.
- Evidence leases and auditing: yes.
- Preventing card accumulation: probably yes, using `ephemeralMessage`.
- Retiring old file reads from provider context: no.

The Antigravity SDK is even more interesting. It exposes transform hooks and context-compaction lifecycle points, but it is currently a research preview and the public documentation does not establish that a hook can replace the complete provider message list. [Antigravity SDK](https://antigravity.google/docs/sdk-overview)

I would prototype Antigravity first.

### Cursor

Cursor now has hooks for prompts, tool activity, responses, subagents and compaction—especially for cloud agents. [Cursor July 2026 update](https://cursor.com/changelog)

However, the documented/current behavior still does not expose a hook that replaces the provider context. `beforeSubmitPrompt` historically could only allow or block, not inject dynamic context. `sessionStart` and `postToolUse` support some context/output shaping, but this still only adds or changes individual content—it does not retire historical messages.

Cursor also performs its own internal pruning and recommends separate chats per task. [Cursor context documentation](https://docs.cursor.com/models)

Verdict: we could build evidence logging, task-boundary detection and a small session card, but not reproduce our measured sawtooth behavior. The recent cloud hook expansion deserves a small capability test because it is only days old, but I would not start the main port there.

### Codex

The current documented Codex customization surfaces—plugins, skills, MCP, `AGENTS.md`, and lifecycle hooks—do not expose the provider message array. Hooks are intended primarily for mechanical lifecycle enforcement around commands, tools and file edits, not model-context replacement. [Current Codex manual](https://developers.openai.com/codex/codex-manual.md)

Therefore, a normal Codex plugin cannot implement the Pi behavior.

There are two viable alternatives:

- Add the necessary context-projection event directly to the open-source Codex CLI core.
- Build a custom Codex-style agent around the OpenAI Responses API/Agents SDK where we own each request’s input.

The second option can provide the full architecture, but it would be our own agent wrapper rather than an ordinary Codex plugin.

### Recommended architecture

We should separate this repository into:

```text
task-card-core
├── transcript/event normalization
├── deterministic extractors
├── evidence leases
├── task boundaries
├── project capabilities
└── projection audits

adapters
├── pi              full context replacement
├── antigravity     ephemeral PreInvocation projection
├── claude          prompt/tool-result shaping
├── cursor          session/tool hook integration
└── codex-wrapper   full projection through owned agent loop
```

My recommendation is:

1. Keep Pi as the reference/full implementation.
2. Port the core to a platform-neutral package.
3. Build an Antigravity `PreInvocation` prototype next.
4. Measure whether ephemeral cards plus Antigravity’s native context handling provide meaningful savings.
5. Treat Cursor, Claude and normal Codex plugins as “task continuity” editions unless they add message-list replacement hooks.

## Benchmark assessment

Ordinary SWE-bench Verified directly addresses the biggest evidence gap: it supplies pinned repositories, real issues, reference fixes, and executable tests. OpenAI now reports frontier performance around 80.9%, while also warning about contamination and flawed tests. Those weaknesses make it unsuitable as a pure capability leaderboard, but a paired A/B experiment can still measure whether context projection preserves correctness while reducing work. [OpenAI’s 2026 assessment](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified/)

SWE-Bench-CL is less aligned than the quoted feedback suggests. It sequences separate, chronological issues to test accumulated experience, transfer, and forgetting. Your spec explicitly says task state expires when a ticket closes and is “not memory.” Carrying knowledge from ticket A into ticket B would test a future research-memory feature—and could violate task isolation—not pinned-plan continuity for one ticket. [SWE-Bench-CL paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00014)

Use the benchmarks this way:

- SWE-bench Verified: primary cross-session correctness experiment.
- SWE-Bench-CL: later test for task isolation or an explicitly gated cross-ticket-memory experiment.
- Terminal-Bench 2.0: useful secondary coverage for terminal behavior, but it does not inherently test cross-session continuity. Its 89 tasks have human solutions and tests, making it a good robustness supplement. [Terminal-Bench 2.0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11868)
- Fresh TS/JS issues: valuable ecological/adoption evidence, but currently open issues are not automatically gradeable. Prefer recently resolved issues pinned before their fixes, or create hidden regression tests.

A clean cross-session SWE-bench protocol would split each issue into:

1. Session 1: receive issue and produce a plan; explicitly pin it.
2. Session 2: resume using the exact issue ID and implement.
3. Session 3: receive the real harness result; diagnose and correct if necessary.

Compare baseline and context-card runs on:

- resolved rate and test results;
- provider input, including cached-input accounting;
- tool calls, errors, duplicate calls, and duration;
- whether the pinned plan and execution facts resume;
- whether zero evidence leases cross the session boundary;
- whether unrelated tasks inherit no prior state.

## Proxy assessment

The core architectural insight is correct: a provider-wire proxy can intercept and replace provider-bound context, satisfying the repository’s adapter eligibility rule at [design-and-evaluation.md](/C:/Users/chkri/source/repos/agent-context-card/docs/design-and-evaluation.md:161). Anthropic officially documents `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` for routing Claude Code through a gateway, including LiteLLM’s Anthropic-format endpoint. [Anthropic gateway documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/llm-gateway)

But it is not only two normalizers:

- Provider requests are stateless and may not carry a stable host session or branch identifier.
- The proxy cannot write Pi custom anchor/audit entries or observe Pi lifecycle events.
- Anthropic system content, tool-use blocks, tool-result pairing, token-count endpoints, prompt-caching headers, and SSE must be preserved.
- Cancellation, backpressure, upstream errors, beta headers, authentication, and streaming usage blocks require transparent pass-through.
- OpenAI support should target the Responses API as well as—or ahead of—legacy Chat Completions for modern coding agents.
- Proxy-local state and audit storage would be a new host-specific layer around the deterministic core.
- Rewriting context may alter provider prompt-cache behavior, so billed cached and uncached tokens must be measured separately.

Yes—the plan is already in the conversation. Requiring the user to restate or explicitly pin it would recreate the bookkeeping burden this project is designed to eliminate.

The better rule is lifecycle-based:

- During a planning turn, keep the exact final assistant response as a plan candidate.
- If the same task continues and the agent begins implementation, automatically promote that candidate to the pinned plan.
- Keep it exact and live until task close.
- If another planning-only turn occurs before further implementation, replace it and mark the plan revision visibly.
- On cross-session resume, persist that exact final planning response with the task state.

The trigger can remain deterministic without interpreting whether prose “looks like a plan.” For example:

> When a settled turn contains no successful mutation, and the next continuation of the same task begins a successful mutation, pin the preceding turn’s final assistant response.

If the host exposes an actual plan-mode or planning lifecycle event, use that stronger signal. Otherwise, the read-only-turn → implementation-turn transition is observable from tool results and requires no user action.

There is a false-positive risk—a design explanation followed by editing could be pinned as a plan—but that is safer than requiring commands and can be measured in the release tests. Also, because completed turns already reduce to the user request plus final assistant response, the necessary source material is naturally available.

**CLI hook route:** Yes, I think it's genuinely valuable, and not just "MCP but worse." MCP requires the *agent's own reasoning* to decide to call a memory tool — it's optional, on-demand. Reproduced and isolated it. Here's what I found:

**Root cause: deterministic greedy decoding with zero repetition penalty**

[LlamaSharpPsmRuntime.cs:231](dotnet/src/PsmMemory.Core/Runtime/LlamaSharpPsmRuntime.cs:231) uses `new GreedySamplingPipeline()` — pure argmax decoding, no `repeat_penalty`/`frequency_penalty`/`no_repeat_ngram`. When the model gets into a local context where the highest-probability next token loops back to a state it's already visited, greedy decoding has no mechanism to break out — it will deterministically repeat forever until `MaxNewTokens` (768) cuts it off. That's exactly the symptom: the raw output shows `"memory":{...}` nesting inside itself identically, over and over, verbatim, until truncation.

**It's not a general backtick/header/list coverage gap — it's specific to this exact text**

I ran three controlled variations against the real Debug/CPU build:

| Variation | Result |
|---|---|
| Original ("Review a pull request", header+list+backticks) | **Fails** — infinite nested loop, `parse_error_noop` |
| Same header+list, backticks removed | Stores correctly (`promote_semantic`) |
| Same list+backticks, header removed | Stores correctly (`promote_semantic`) |
| Different topic ("Deploy a service"), same header+list+backticks shape | Stores correctly (`ignore`, cleanly parsed) |

So the shape itself (H1 + numbered list + code spans) is fine — only this specific PR-review text triggers it.

**Suspicious clue**: the degenerate output's tags include `"prod_eval_id:workflow-review-pr","prod_version":"1.4"` — literal training-pipeline artifact tags. Grepping the repo's training-adjacent data, `workflow-review-pr` shows up in `psm-model/prod-memory/results/coding-agent-candidate-turns.jsonl` — not as a proper stored-memory example, but as a **mention** of a test fixture name inside a meta-conversation about PSM's own eval regressions (a Claude Code session discussing `workflow-review-pr` as a failing fixture). This suggests the model has partially memorized/overfit on a near-duplicate or corrupted training row tied to this specific text, and the greedy sampler turns that local confusion into an unbounded loop instead of a graceful mistake.

I couldn't fully close the loop on which exact training row is responsible — the Coding storage adapter (`hf-prod-storage-v16b-qwen0.5b`) was trained from a dataset not present locally under `psm-model/prod-memory/data/` (only conversational-domain jsonls are there); its source data likely lives on the training pod/HF.

**Recommendation**: the highest-leverage, lowest-risk fix is adding a repetition penalty (or `no_repeat_ngram`) to `GreedySamplingPipeline` in `LlamaSharpPsmRuntime.cs` — that caps this failure mode generically regardless of root cause, without touching training data. The tradeoff is it changes generation for every call, so it'd need a gate re-run (per your [Gate eval on pod](psm-model/prod-memory/checkpoints) convention, ~2 min on GPU) to confirm no regression on the 419-case holdout before promoting.

No — let me be precise about what exists vs. what doesn't, since I think my last message conflated them.

**What's already built:** the *pattern* of "load once, serve many requests" exists in two places:
1. `PsmMemory.Mcp`'s `Program.cs` — loads the model once at startup, stays warm for the life of that process.
2. The CLI's `serve` NDJSON mode — same idea, one process, one model load, many requests piped through stdin.

**What's missing:** a way for a *brand-new, independent* process to reach either of those already-running ones. Both of the above are only warm for whoever is *already connected to their specific pipe* — the MCP client that spawned the MCP process, or whatever spawned `serve` and is feeding it stdin. `hook recall` is invoked as `psm-memory hook recall` — a fresh OS process, launched fresh by the agent harness on every turn, with no pipe connection to any pre-existing process. It has no way to find or talk to an already-warm model even if one happens to be running elsewhere on the machine. So today, `hook recall` always does `LlamaSharpPsmRuntime.CreateAsync(...)` from scratch, every single call.

The daemon is specifically the missing piece that solves *that* gap: a small standalone process that stays warm and listens on a loopback port (or similar), so `hook recall` can check "is one already running? if not, start one" and then just make a fast local request to it instead of loading the model itself. That rendezvous mechanism doesn't exist yet in the C# port — that's the actual gap, not the warm-loading pattern itself, which is already proven out twice.

**Why MCP and CLI each do it their own way — the actual constraint, not an excuse:** an in-memory loaded model can't be shared across OS process boundaries in .NET (or any runtime) without some IPC mechanism — that part is a hard constraint, not sloppiness. Each host just directly calls `LlamaSharpPsmRuntime.CreateAsync` itself and lives with the result. That's the actual bug: model lifecycle management is missing from Core entirely, not inconsistently implemented in it.

Pi does not select a provider account directly. It selects a model ID and sends that ID to the router. The router then chooses the account behind that model.

For example, if Pi selects:

```json
{ "model": "@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct" }
```

the current router:

1. Looks for an exact routing rule for that model.
2. If none exists, finds enabled accounts advertising that exact model ID.
3. Orders those accounts by `Priority`.
4. Sends the request through the first account.
5. For non-streaming requests, moves to the next account only if the current one fails.

With two Cloudflare accounts that both expose the model:

```text
Pi selects @cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct
  → Cloudflare Account A, priority 1
  → Cloudflare Account B, priority 2, only if A fails
```

The accounts are not round-robined. Despite the `RoundRobin` enum existing, current behavior is priority-based failover.

For two Ollama accounts exposing the same model:

```text
Pi selects qwen2.5-coder:32b
  → Ollama Account A, priority 1
  → Ollama Account B, priority 2, only if A fails
```

Important limitations

- Pi’s exported `models.json` contains a distinct union of model IDs. It does not expose individual accounts.
- Account selection is therefore invisible to Pi.
- Failover requires the next account to accept the same model ID.
- The router currently does not translate model names between providers. It cannot automatically map:

```text
@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct
    ↓
llama3.1:8b
```

- An explicit routing rule controls account order, but it still passes the original model ID unchanged.
- Streaming currently uses only the first selected account and does not retry another account after failure.
- After three failures, an account enters a two-minute cooldown.
- Prompt-cache hits bypass provider selection entirely.

For your example

Suppose you configure:

| Account | Models | Priority |
|---|---|---:|
| Cloudflare A | `@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct` | 1 |
| Cloudflare B | `@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct` | 2 |
| Ollama A | `llama3.1:8b` | 3 |
| Ollama B | `llama3.1:8b` | 4 |

Selecting the Cloudflare model in Pi only uses Cloudflare A/B. Selecting `llama3.1:8b` only uses Ollama A/B. It will not cross from Cloudflare to Ollama because their model identifiers differ.

What the router needs for seamless cross-provider switching is a route-target mapping such as:

```text
Pi model alias: coding-llama

1. Cloudflare A → @cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct
2. Cloudflare B → @cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct
3. Ollama A     → llama3.1:8b
4. Ollama B     → llama3.1:8b
```

Each fallback entry needs both an account ID and that account’s target model ID. The current [`RoutingRule`](C:/Users/chkri/source/repos/AIInferenceRouter/src/AIInferenceRouter.Entities/Models/RoutingRule.cs) stores only account IDs, so true cross-provider model aliases are not implemented yet.

## What must change

The current router cannot do this correctly because [`RoutingRule`](C:/Users/chkri/source/repos/AIInferenceRouter/src/AIInferenceRouter.Entities/Models/RoutingRule.cs) stores only account IDs. It does not store a different target model for each account.

It needs route targets shaped approximately like:

```json
{
  "alias": "daily-coder",
  "targets": [
    {
      "providerAccountId": 1,
      "targetModelId": "qwen3-coder:480b-cloud"
    },
    {
      "providerAccountId": 2,
      "targetModelId": "@cf/qwen/qwen3-coder"
    },
    {
      "providerAccountId": 3,
      "targetModelId": "qwen3-coder:480b-cloud"
    },
    {
      "providerAccountId": 4,
      "targetModelId": "@cf/qwen/qwen3-coder"
    }
  ]
}
```

For every target, the router must clone the Pi request and replace:

```json
{ "model": "daily-coder" }
```

with that target’s real model ID.

## Quota-aware failover

Not every HTTP `429` means the same thing, so the router should classify provider failures.

- Cloudflare error `3036` means the daily 10,000-neuron allocation is exhausted. That account should be disabled until the next 00:00 UTC reset. [Cloudflare errors](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/errors/), [Cloudflare pricing and reset time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/pricing/).
- Cloudflare error `3040` means temporary capacity exhaustion. That should receive a short cooldown, not a full-day suspension.
- Ollama documents `429` as rate-limit exhaustion but does not publish a universal reset schedule. The router should honor `Retry-After` when present and otherwise use a configurable account cooldown. [Ollama API errors](https://docs.ollama.com/api/errors).
- Authentication, invalid-model, and malformed-request errors should not be treated as quota exhaustion.

The provider adapters therefore need to throw a structured exception containing:

```text
HTTP status
provider error code
response body
Retry-After
account ID
target model ID
```

Then the router can apply the correct policy immediately instead of its current “three failures, then two-minute cooldown” behavior.

## Streaming is important for Pi

Pi normally consumes streaming responses. The current router only attempts the first account for streaming requests, so your desired workflow currently will not work reliably even if a routing rule contains multiple accounts.

Streaming failover must:

1. Start the first provider request.
2. If it fails before emitting any tokens, mark its quota/cooldown and try the next target.
3. Once any token has been delivered to Pi, do not restart on another provider because that could duplicate or corrupt the response.
4. Record which physical account/model handled the request.

The exported `models.json` should expose the stable alias:

Pi continues sending `daily-coder` all day. Account rotation, provider changes, cooldowns, and target-model translation stay entirely inside the router.

The route aliases should be exported alongside—or instead of—the raw discovered provider model IDs. That gives you one dependable Pi model entry rather than four physical entries you must switch manually.

In short: the right solution is not account switching inside Pi. It is alias-based, per-account model mapping plus quota-aware streaming failover inside the router.

The problem is not pinning the plan. Pinning works:

1. Planning turn captures the exact plan.
2. The next session promotes it and projects it.
3. The plan remains available across sessions.

The failure is acting on a pinned plan when it contains temporary planning instructions such as “do not modify files.” Nano treats that old constraint as still active during implementation.

So the real design gap is:

> How do we preserve the exact plan while distinguishing durable steps from phase-scoped instructions?

The robust target is a structured plan like:

```text
Durable steps:
- Update counter.mjs
- Run increment tests

Planning-only constraints:
- Do not modify files while investigating
- Do not run mutating commands during planning
```

When implementation begins, durable steps remain active; planning-only constraints become historical metadata. The scope-note experiment showed that merely adding a disclaimer is not reliable enough.

So: keep pinning, redesign plan authority across lifecycle phases.

You’re mostly right, with one important distinction.

There are two separate things:

1. Pi’s plan-mode constraint: a host/system-level instruction such as “do not edit files.” This applies to the planning request. Switching modes does not necessarily create a new conversation; it may simply change the instructions sent with later requests.

2. The assistant’s plan response: the ordinary assistant message containing the proposed steps. Our extension captures that response and stores it as a pinned artifact for later sessions.

The problem is that the assistant often repeats the plan-mode constraint inside its own plan:

```text
Do not modify files.
1. Inspect counter.mjs
2. Implement the fix
```

When we later pin and project that text, Pi’s original plan-mode metadata may be gone, but the sentence remains inside the assistant-authored artifact. Nano then treats it as an active instruction.

So the plan is independently stored, but not semantically independent: its text contains an instruction inherited from the earlier mode.

The required distinction is:

```text
Host plan-mode constraint:
  planning-only; expires at implementation

Pinned durable plan:
  remains active across sessions
```

Our current system preserves the second exactly, but does not separate it from the first when the assistant has copied the constraint into its response.

I dug into the actual `raw_output` text and validation `issues` for both domains (not just the aggregate scores), and the picture is much clearer than the scary numbers suggested:

```
raw model output: {"action":"store_episodic","memory":{"content":"Caroline attended a LGBTQ support group."},"facts":[...]}
eval records:      action: "ignore"   ← forced fail-safe, because validation rejected the missing fields
```

The model's actual judgment is contextually sensible in the samples I checked — it's not garbage. But every "would-store" decision gets validated against a stricter schema than it was trained to produce, fails, and falls back to `ignore`. The installed Pi is `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` version `0.82.1`, not the commonly referenced upstream package. Its real API provides:

- `ctx.mode`, including `"print"`
- `ctx.cwd`
- `ctx.sessionManager.getSessionId()`
- `before_agent_start`, with the expanded prompt and system prompt
- `agent_start`, `agent_end`, and `agent_settled`
- Tool execution events
- `session_start` and `session_shutdown`
- Runtime custom-tool registration
- TypeBox validation
- Global extensions at `~/.pi/agent/extensions/`

### Recommended design changes

1. Use a new UUID for each invocation

Pi’s session ID is a UUIDv7, but it is a session identity—not an invocation identity. `--session`, `--continue`, and `--session-id` can reuse it.

I recommend:

```json
{
  "workerId": "<fresh random UUID>",
  "piSessionId": "<native Pi session ID>"
}
```

This guarantees that concurrent invocations never collide while retaining the useful native identifier. Use the flat layout:

```text
.pi/workers/<workerId>/progress.json
```

Pi exposes no reliable parent/orchestrator identity, so a parent hierarchy should not be invented.

2. Register the tool only in print mode

Pi 0.82.1 supports registering tools during `session_start`. Therefore:

```typescript
pi.on("session_start", (_event, ctx) => {
  if (ctx.mode !== "print") return;
  // Register update_progress
});
```

This is cleaner than globally registering the tool and trying to deactivate it. Interactive sessions get no tool, no injected instruction, and no filesystem writes.

3. Let the extension own terminal status

The model should only be able to report:

- `working`
- `blocked`

The extension should exclusively assign:

- `starting`
- `done`
- `failed`

Otherwise the model could mark itself `done` before its final response or mark a recoverable provider retry as failed.

4. Finalize on `agent_settled`, not immediately on `agent_end`

Pi can retry or compact after `agent_end`. `agent_settled` explicitly means no automatic retry, compaction, or queued continuation remains.

Recommended logic:

- Capture the last assistant message and its `stopReason` during `agent_end`.
- Finalize during `agent_settled`.
- `error` or `aborted` → `failed`.
- Normal stop → `done`.
- If `session_shutdown` occurs before settling, mark it failed/interrupted when possible.

Abrupt process kills may bypass shutdown hooks; that limitation should be documented.

5. Avoid automatic semantic inference from shell commands

Turning tool commands into progress descriptions risks:

- Leaking command text into the snapshot
- Producing misleading “current work”
- Writing far too frequently
- Accidentally recording sensitive arguments

Lifecycle hooks should manage initial and terminal state. A compact `update_progress` tool should supply semantic intermediate state.

6. Bound all model-provided data

Use TypeBox limits such as:

- Maximum number of completed/pending items
- Maximum length per item
- Maximum `current` and blocker lengths
- A maximum task-preview length

### 1. A blocking `pi -p` cannot be monitored by the same execution thread

If the orchestrator runs:

```bash

```

synchronously, it cannot inspect progress until Pi exits. Even knowing the worker ID would not help—the orchestrator is blocked.

Progress monitoring requires the orchestrator’s execution mechanism to:

- Start Pi asynchronously or in the background.
- Return a process/job handle.
- Continue issuing other commands while Pi runs.

For example, conceptually:

```text

start pi asynchronously
inspect .pi/workers/<worker-id>/progress.json when needed
wait for process completion
```

If the orchestration tool only supports blocking execution, neither snapshot files nor JSON mode can provide interactive monitoring to that same orchestrator turn.

### 2. JSON mode does not solve the blocking problem

JSON mode provides events:

```bash
pi --mode json "<task>"
```

But the orchestrator must still consume the process asynchronously. It also has notable drawbacks:

- Streams many events instead of one compact state.
- Includes messages, tool events, and potentially substantial output.
- Requires the parent to continuously parse and reduce the stream.
- Risks exactly the context pollution this extension is meant to avoid.
- Still does not intrinsically establish which events belong to which higher-level orchestrator task.

We could redirect JSON to a file and run a reducer, but then we would be rebuilding a more complicated version of the progress extension.

The extension can retrieve the same value through:

```typescript

I’m treating this as a clean, reusable tool and will keep the dangerous parts explicit: a job gets a hard timeout, a no-progress timeout, remote process/heartbeat checks, and cleanup in a `finally` path so an agent cannot “wait forever.” I’m also verifying the current RunPod API rather than baking in stale endpoint assumptions.

The key design decision is to use the official `runpodctl pod create --terminate-after …` for provisioning. That gives every newly created pod a RunPod-side hard expiry even if the agent, terminal, SSH session, or local runner crashes. The runner will add a second in-pod watchdog after SSH connects, plus local cleanup—three independent cost-safety layers.
